title: Why End of the Road Remains the Shining Star of the U.K.’s Indie Festival Scene After 20 Years: ‘Don’t Offer the Same Old Thing’
summary: Geese, Pulp, CMAT and Mac DeMarco topped this year's bill. Founder Simon Taffe explains how the event came together and has retained its charm.
contentText:
For the past 20 years, attendees at End of the Road festival in southwest England have become accustomed to expecting the unexpected. Secret sets from big name acts, hidden areas on the site and last-minute, impromptu moments of magic are par for the course at this haven for fans of alternative and independent music.

Case in point: Prior to an unannounced set by red-hot Irish trad-folk band Madra Salach on the Saturday afternoon of 2026’s event (Sept. 5), one punter took it upon herself to keep the waiting crowd entertained by playing an empty piano on stage before the band began soundchecking. When she finished her first piece, a fellow attendee approached to ask if she could continue playing in the background while he recited one of his own poems — one about a rock’n’roll grandma that’s lived a life of adventure and love. She tinkled the ivories while he talked tenderly of her life, reading to 50 engrossed strangers. This wasn’t the performance we’d come to see, but it was one emblematic of the festival’s whole ethos: throw yourself into everything and embrace connection.

End of the Road is full of magical moments like this, where attendees are active participants in crafting and maintaining a truly special atmosphere. In the Effing Forest section of the site, unique artworks and installations encourage children and grown-ups alike to get involved with poetry workshops and botanical screenprinting, and to contribute to the festival’s creative atmosphere.

It’s a feeling that seeps into the music performances, too. Sunday’s headliner CMAT says that this is her favourite festival because it “features basically all the music I listen to all year,” while Mac DeMarco namechecks festival co-founder Simon Taffe and thanks him for inviting him back after a near-decade absence. Pulp wrapped their 18-month world tour at the festival, using the opportunity to play rarities and deep cuts, some for the first time ever. This is not just another stop on the festival circuit for these acts, but the main event. 

Burak Cingi

End of the Road began at Larmer Tree Gardens on the border of Dorset and Wiltshire in 2006. Co-founders Taffe and Sophia Hagberg were inspired by the All Tomorrow’s Parties model, which encouraged artists to curate the lineup and create an all-encompassing world for fans. It was Taffe’s “way into music” beyond just playing in “s–t indie bands” and an alternative to his career in decorating and construction. (Hagberg eventually retired as a director in 2015)

Early plans were rudimentary but frugal planning – and blind ambition – gave him an insight into what is actually required to run the festival. He sold his house to finance the first edition, and convinced a friend to remortgage his house to add to the pot: the total he borrowed came to £160,000 ($216,000). “I thought if I lost everything, it would take me like another six, seven years to get back to where I am. I could build it back again,” he tells Billboard U.K. “What’s the worst that could happen?”

They shifted 5000 passes in their first year, with a line-up that featured Badly Drawn Boy and Ryan Adams (Taffe admits that a chunk were given to competition entrants and a disproportionate amount ended up winning). Each year grew steadily, with the third edition featuring 6,000 guests; now, it’s up to 15,000 devoted attendees. Its name is a nod to the fact that it brings a swansong to the U.K.’s summer of festivals.

Over the years End of the Road has given early headlining opportunities to rising acts (Tame Impala, Father John Misty), earned bookings of contemporary stars (Vampire Weekend, Fleet Foxes, St Vincent and Mac DeMarco) and bagged legends (Patti Smith). Future stars like Fontaines D.C., Japanese Breakfast, Alex G, and Mitski all played the festival’s smaller stages on their journeys. The stacked 2026 bill also included sets from Geese, Angine de Poitrine, Super Furry Animals, Fat Dog, Earl Sweatshirt & Mike and Kurt Vile.

“We’ve always tried to punch above our weight and give more,” Taffe says of his team’s approach to curation. “I’ve wanted to create that sense that the artists really feel involved and looked after and to be a place that’s going to inspire people.” He points to indie group Wet Leg, who formed after a revelatory End of the Road experience; the festival is a regular sell-out, with a majority snapped up in early bird presales.

Maintaining that ethos has meant bold decisions have been taken over the years. “Without mentioning names, we turn down lots of bands and artists that would sell out a festival in two minutes,” Taffe laughs. The dream headliner wishlist is punchy and ambitious: Tom Waits, Nick Cave, PJ Harvey, and Neil Young are all targets for Taffe’s team. That commitment extends to the whole bill, and he never wants to “ruin the festival vibe over a single booking.” Acts selected have to meet a strict criteria: would Taffe want to pay for their music on vinyl, or a ticket to see them?

The festival remains fiercely independent, a beacon for what is possible away from the corporate giants. According to the Association of Independent Festivals , Live Nation currently owns or controls 24% of the U.K. market, including events like Reading & Leeds, Download, and Latitude. AEG Presents and Superstruct also have a substantial footprint throughout the market.

Taffe says he has “batted away” offers to purchase the festival because “it’s worth more to me than it ever can to them.” It means that the limited partners that are brought into the festival are done so thoughtfully, and brand activations are a non-starter. Instead, retailers and labels such as Rough Trade and Third Man Records set up pop-up record shops for attendees to flick through and buy LPs from acts they’ve just seen perform. Tastemakers such as indie publication So Young and promoters Bird on the Wire are invited to curate and collaborate, not just to badge existing stages.

Being independent has its benefits and drawbacks: they can remain flexible and cocksure on their vision, but the market’s current outlook does not make them immune to challenges. The AIF reports that since 2019, 300 festivals have closed in the U.K. owing to rising costs such as security, labor and infrastructure. 

Speaking to Ticket Tailor , the association’s CEO Jon Rostron said that in he post-COVID landscape, the market was beginning to settle, and that independent festivals play a huge part in the ecosystem. “There’s somewhere in the region of at least 600 music festivals in the UK. The big ones are owned by the corporations, but the majority of festivals are independent. That long tail that goes all the way down. So they’re really, really important, because they are where most people go.”

Taffe concurs and says that End of the Road is in a healthy place as a business and supports seven full-time staff and hundreds of contractors in the run-up to the event. The strength of the vision and mission ensures a relatively steady business. “I don’t think there’s many people doing what we do,” he says. “I’ve had the team worry about festivals that have come and gone that have been trying to do similar things and it hasn’t worked. But I just stay in my lane, do my own thing. You have to offer something unique and you can’t just put the same line-up that’s on down the road.”

It’s a festival that operates in a sweet spot: expansion is not on the horizon and the relationship with the operators of Larmer Tree Gardens is secure for the years to come. The character of the venue is key, with The Garden Stage incorporating the character of the grounds, once a privately-owned venue in the Victorian age. The Singing Theatre, a freestanding stage with a painted backdrop, hosts late-night discos, while peacocks roam the grounds.
